lead: A temperature difference between top and bottom is built-in curvature. A free beam bows with no stress. Stress appears only when curvature or axial extension is restrained. Sun heating an upper wing skin while the lower skin stays cool is one aircraft case. Only a few universities teach this. A bimetallic strip uses the same idea with two expansion coefficients.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for curvature and plane sections.

blocks.text: For a linear rise, ΔT(y) = ΔT<sub>mean</sub> + k y. y is depth from mid-depth in m; k is the gradient in K/m; ΔT<sub>mean</sub> is defined in Section 2. Free thermal strain is ε<sub>T</sub> = αΔT, with α in per K. Aluminium has α ≈ 23 × 10<sup>−6</sup> per K.
Plane sections stay plane. The free strain difference from bottom to top is α(ΔT<sub>top</sub> − ΔT<sub>bottom</sub>). Over depth h this is the free thermal curvature:

blocks.where: R<sub>T</sub> is the free radius in m; h is the depth in m; temperatures are in K. The hot face becomes convex: mid-span moves toward the hot side, and the ends curl toward the cooler side. No stress is needed, so σ = 0.

blocks.text: If curvature is prevented, sections stay straight. Let the total axial strain be ε<sub>0</sub>, uniform through the depth. The stress is σ(y) = E[ε<sub>0</sub> − αΔT(y)], with E in Pa. If the ends are free axially, ∫σ dA = 0, so ε<sub>0</sub> = αΔT<sub>mean</sub>. Here ΔT<sub>mean</sub> is the area-average rise, ∫ΔT dA/A; for a section symmetric about mid-depth with a linear gradient it equals the mid-depth value. Then

blocks.where: σ(y) is axial stress in Pa; E is Young's modulus in Pa; α is in per K; ΔT<sub>mean</sub> is the area-average rise in K; ΔT(y) is the local rise in K. The resultant force is zero, so no net axial load is needed. But the stress has a net moment of magnitude EαkI, which the restraint must supply. It is not self-equilibrating. Only when both force and moment resultants are zero (for example a non-linear gradient in a free beam) is the stress self-equilibrating. The stress is zero at mid-depth. At the surfaces σ = ∓EαΔT/2, where ΔT is the top-to-bottom difference. The hot face is in compression.

blocks.text: If the ends are also held against axial extension while curvature is prevented, ε<sub>0</sub> = 0 and σ(y) = −EαΔT(y).

items: Sun on the upper wing skin with a cool lower skin gives a spar gradient.
A hot bleed-air duct heats one side of a fuselage frame; clips and skin restrain the bow.
A bimetallic strip: free, it bends; held straight, it develops stress.

figure.caption: Temperature rises linearly from 5 K at the bottom to 35 K at the top. With curvature held, stress changes sign at mid-depth and reaches about 24 MPa compression at the hot face. Read the ΔT curve in K and the stress curve in MPa; they only share the plotted scale.

y.label: value (ΔT in K; stress in MPa)

spec.aria: Temperature rises linearly from 5 K at the bottom to 35 K at the top of a 100 mm deep spar. With curvature prevented, stress changes sign through mid-depth and reaches about 24 MPa compression at the hot face. Read ΔT in K and stress in MPa.

examples.question: An aluminium spar is 100 mm deep. E = 70 GPa and α = 23 × 10<sup>−6</sup> per K. The top flange is 35 °C and the bottom flange is 5 °C. Find (a) the free radius and (b) the surface stresses if curvature is prevented but axial extension is free.
steps: Surface stress magnitude is EαΔT/2. Half the top-to-bottom difference is 15 K.
Sign: hot top face −24.15 MPa (compression); cool bottom face +24.15 MPa (tension).
examples.answer: R<sub>T</sub> = 145 m; surface stresses are −24.15 MPa on the hot top face and +24.15 MPa on the cool bottom face.
examples.check:
E=70e9
alpha=23e-6
h=0.100
dT=35-5
curv=alpha*dT/h
R=1/curv
sigma=E*alpha*dT/2
print(round(curv,4))
print(round(R,1))
print(round(sigma/1e6,2))

traps: Using σ = EαΔT on a free beam. A free beam bows stress-free; only restraint gives stress.
Forgetting the factor 1/2. Surface stress is EαΔT/2 for a linear gradient.
Wrong sign: with curvature held, the hot face is in compression.
Using a uniform rise in the gradient formula. A free uniform rise gives no stress unless axial extension is restrained.
Putting h in mm. Convert to m before curvature per metre.

quiz.q: State the formula for free thermal curvature of a beam with a linear temperature gradient.
quiz.a: 1/R<sub>T</sub> = α(ΔT<sub>top</sub> − ΔT<sub>bottom</sub>)/h, with h in m and temperatures in K.

quiz.q: A free beam has a linear temperature gradient and bends. Why is the stress zero?
quiz.a: The free thermal strain varies linearly and fits plane sections. The beam bows without elastic strain; stress depends on mechanical strain.

quiz.q: An aluminium spar is 80 mm deep, E = 72 GPa, α = 23 × 10<sup>−6</sup> per K. Top flange 40 °C, bottom 10 °C. Curvature is prevented but axial extension is free. Find the free radius and the surface stresses with signs.
quiz.a: ΔT = 30 K, h = 0.080 m. 1/R<sub>T</sub> = 23 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 30 / 0.080 = 8.625 × 10<sup>−3</sup> per m, so R<sub>T</sub> = 115.9 m. σ = ±EαΔT/2 = ±72 × 10<sup>9</sup> × 23 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 15 = ±24.84 MPa. Hot top flange: −24.84 MPa (compression). Cool bottom flange: +24.84 MPa (tension).

quiz.q: A spar has curvature prevented and both ends held against axial extension. The mean temperature rise is 25 K. Write the stress at mid-depth and state its sign.
quiz.a: With both restraints, σ = −EαΔT(y). At mid-depth ΔT = 25 K, so σ = −Eα × 25 K. It is compressive because the heated material is held from expanding.

quiz.q: What does α measure and what is its unit?
quiz.a: α is the coefficient of thermal expansion: free strain per kelvin of temperature rise, unit 1/K.

quiz.q: A steel spar 120 mm deep has E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10<sup>−6</sup> per K, and a top-to-bottom difference of 40 K. Find the surface stress when curvature is prevented.
quiz.a: σ = ±EαΔT/2 = 200 × 10<sup>9</sup> × 12 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × 20 = 48 MPa. The hot face is in compression.

beyond: Not for the exam. Composite wing skins have plies with different α, so a laminate can cure with built-in stress. Aeroheating adds transient gradients and thermal fatigue. Search for thermal stress in laminated plates, thermal buckling, and aeroheating.
